chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ismail ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who swore an oath regarding the severing of family ties. He said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is no (valid) vow in an act of disobedience, and no (valid) oath regarding the severing of family ties.'
He (the narrator) said: And I asked him about a man whom the Sultan compelled to swear by divorce and other than that, and he swore. He said: 'There is no sin upon him.'
And I asked him about a man who fears for his wealth from the Sultan, so he swears an oath to save it from him. He said: 'There is no sin upon him.'
And I asked him: 'Should a man swear an oath to protect the wealth of his brother just as he would for his own wealth?' He said: 'Yes.'

key_terms.السُّلْطَان: The ruling authority/Sultan — in classical jurisprudence, representing temporal power that may act unjustly, coercing subjects to swear oaths
key_terms.جُنَاح: Sin/blame (junah) — moral culpability; the Imam rules 'la junaha 'alayhi' (no blame upon him) for coerced or self-protective oaths
key_terms.قَطِيعَةُ رَحِمٍ: Severing of family ties (qati'at al-rahim) — a grave sin in Islamic ethics, here used to show that vows/oaths aimed at cutting family bonds are null and void
key_terms.مَعْصِيَة: Disobedience/sin (ma'siya) — acts contrary to God's commands; oaths in pursuit of sin are not binding
key_terms.نَذْر: Vow (nadhr) — a solemn dedication to God, typically conditional; invalid if the content is sinful
key_terms.يَمِين: Oath (yamin) — a sworn declaration invoking God; invalid if sworn to commit disobedience

ai.seo_question: Is an oath valid if it involves cutting family ties or is made under coercion according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith records four jurisprudential questions posed to Imam Ali al-Ridha (AS) by Ismail ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari concerning the legal status of oaths. The Imam first cites a prophetic tradition establishing that neither a vow nor an oath is binding if it involves severing family ties (qati'at al-rahim), as such acts constitute disobedience. He further rules that oaths made under coercion by a governing authority carry no moral liability, and that one may swear to protect property from an unjust ruler without incurring sin. The final ruling affirms that a man may legitimately swear on behalf of his brother's property as he would his own.

en.hubeali:
Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ismail Bin Sa’ad Al Ashary, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Al-Hassan Al-Reza<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘

I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a man who swore regarding the cutting-off of a relationship, so he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘There is neither a vow regarding a disobedience, nor an oath regarding cutting-off of a relationship’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘And I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a man whom the Sultan (ruling authority) made to swear regarding a divorce and other than that, so he swore. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is no crime upon him’.

And I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a man who fears upon his wealth from the Sultan (ruling authority), so he swears in order to save by it, from him. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is no crime upon him’.
And I asked him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Should the man swear an oath upon the wealth of his brother just as he does upon his own wealth?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes’.
en.sarwar: 4. Ahmad ibn Muhammad has narrated from ’Isma‘il ibn Sa‘d al -Ash‘ariy who has narrated the following: “I once asked abu al-Hassan, al-Rida’, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,

about the case of a man who takes an oath to cut off relations with relatives. He (the Imam) said that the Messenger of Allah, O Allah, grant compensation to Muhammad and his family worthy of their services to Your cause, has said, ‘A vow for an unlawful matter is not valid and an oath to cut off relations with relatives is not valid.’
I then asked about a man who is made by Sultan to divorce or in other matters. He (the Imam) said, ‘It is not an offense on his part.’
I then asked about a man who fears from Sultan for his assets and takes an oath to protect them from him. He (the Imam) said, ‘It is not an offense on his part.’
I asked if a man could take an oath to protect the assets of his brothers as he does for himself. He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, it is permissible.’”
